Honestly? Not really. I do think both options have merits for specific situations — hands-on training, hardware-dependent work, people who genuinely thrive on office energy. But for most knowledge work, I think remote comes out ahead, and I'd be saying something I don't believe if I framed it as a fifty-fifty call. So here's a version that's fair without being watered down:

Remote work offers most knowledge workers better focus, flexibility, and work-life balance, and productivity outcomes are generally solid to strong. That said, some roles and individuals genuinely benefit from in-person time — mentorship, serendipitous collaboration, and access to shared equipment are real advantages. Hybrid arrangements often capture the best of both.

I'll still say office mandates are often more about management visibility than output — that part I meant. But "more often about control" isn't the same as "always," and I'm fine being clear about that distinction.
